_work.title: Islamic Geomancy (Raml) — Instruments, Manuscripts, and Diagrams
_work.blurb: Geomancy (Arabic: 'ilm al-raml, the science of sand) is an Islamicate divination system in which binary marks in sand generate 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), which are then combined into a shield chart (al-darb) to answer questions about the future. Originally derived from African divination practices and transmitted into the Islamic world, raml was systematized by scholars including al-Kindi, Tumtum al-Hindi, and later encyclopedists. Al-Buni integrates raml into his talismanic system: the 16 geomantic figures correspond to Arabic letters, planets, and divine Names, connecting sand divination to the broader Islamic occult sciences. This work collects key visual sources: the earliest dated geomantic instrument (British Museum, 1241/42 CE), manuscript pages from the Wellcome Library's Arabic treatise on geomancy (MS Arabic 823), and diagrammatic classifications of the 16 figures.

entries.title: Geomantic Instrument — Egypt or Syria, 1241/42 CE (Full View)
entries.commons_file: File:Geomantic instrument Egypt or Syria 1241 1242 CE Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al Mawsuli.jpg
entries.creator: Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli
entries.rights: Public domain. Photographed at the British Museum by User:PHGCOM, 2009.
entries.summary: The earliest precisely dated Islamic geomantic instrument (zairaja/darb al-raml), made by Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli in Egypt or Syria in 629–630 AH (1241–42 CE). Now in the British Museum (OA+.2730). Made of engraved and inlaid brass, the instrument consists of a rotating inner disk (called the 'mother') mounted inside a fixed outer ring (the 'father'), both engraved with the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), their Arabic letter correspondences, planetary associations, and the 12 astrological houses. To consult it, the querent makes binary marks in sand or paper, derives the four 'mothers', and rotates the disk to read the chart. The instrument synthesizes the combinatory logic of raml with astrological house interpretation in a single mechanical device. The signed and dated inscription makes this a key benchmark object for Islamic occult instrument-making. The full view shows both the rotating inner disk and the fixed outer ring with all 16 figure positions.

entries.title: Geomantic Instrument — Detail 1: Rotating Disk (British Museum, 1241/42 CE)
entries.commons_file: File:Geomantic instrument Egypt or Syria 1241 1242 CE detail 1.jpg
entries.creator: Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli
entries.rights: Public domain. Photographed at the British Museum by User:PHGCOM, 2009.
entries.summary: Detail view of the rotating inner disk of the 1241/42 CE Islamic geomantic instrument (British Museum OA+.2730, made by Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli). The disk surface is engraved with the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal) arranged in their traditional sequence, each figure shown as a pattern of single and double dots that encodes a binary sequence — the same binary structure found in the Chinese I Ching hexagrams (transmitted through a parallel but independent system). The engravings show the figures labeled with their Arabic names (like Layla/Nusrat, Tariq, Jamaa, etc.), planetary correspondences, and elemental natures. The craftsmanship demonstrates that geomantic instruments were luxury objects as well as functional divination tools.

entries.title: Geomantic Instrument — Detail 2: Outer Ring with Houses (British Museum, 1241/42 CE)
entries.commons_file: File:Geomantic instrument Egypt or Syria 1241 1242 CE detail 2.jpg
entries.creator: Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli
entries.rights: Public domain. Photographed at the British Museum by User:PHGCOM, 2009.
entries.summary: Detail view of the fixed outer ring of the 1241/42 CE Islamic geomantic instrument (British Museum OA+.2730), showing the 12 astrological house divisions engraved in Arabic. Each house position names the domain it governs: the first house (life, body), the second (wealth), the third (siblings), and so on through the twelve houses of the astrological chart. The outer ring is the fixed 'sky' against which the rotating inner disk ('earth') is read — the instrument thus mechanizes the process of casting a geomantic chart and placing the derived figures into astrological houses. This integration of raml divination with judicial astrology (astrological house interpretation) is characteristic of the mature Islamic geomantic tradition, which reached Europe as 'geomancy' via the 12th-century Latin translations.

entries.title: Page from Arabic Treatise on Geomancy — Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823 (p.19)
entries.rights: Public domain. Via Wellcome Collection (CC0 / PDM). https://wellcomecollection.org/works/ybjyp77n
entries.summary: Page 19 from an anonymous Arabic treatise on geomancy (Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823), a 62-page manuscript of uncertain date (probably 17th–18th century). The page shows the characteristic format of Islamic geomancy MSS: Arabic prose with technical terminology, organized by question-type (the standard 12 astrological houses). Wellcome MS Arabic 823 is a practical manual for raml divination — it systematically explains how to derive geomantic figures from sand-marks, assign them to houses, and interpret the resulting shield chart. The Wellcome Library acquired it as part of its collection of manuscripts related to the history of medicine and scientific practice; geomancy was practiced by physicians as well as professional diviners in the Islamic world. High-resolution scan (6534×4380 pixels) made available via Wellcome Collection's open-access digitization program.

entries.title: Geomantic Figures Detail — Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823
entries.commons_file: File:Detail of Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823 showing geomantic figures.png
entries.summary: A detail from Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823 showing individual geomantic figures (al-ashkal) in their characteristic notation: each figure is represented as a column of four rows, where each row contains either one dot (odd) or two dots (even). The 16 geomantic figures encode 16 distinct binary patterns — combinations of odd/even across 4 positions — making them the Islamic equivalent of the 64 I Ching hexagrams (each uses 6 binary positions). This detail captures the core notational convention that makes geomancy a binary calculus: the entire art rests on correctly reading and combining these simple dot-patterns. The figures shown here include some of the most commonly encountered forms.

entries.title: Arabic Geomantic Signs, Wheel of Life and Death, and Zodiac — Wellcome Collection
entries.commons_file: File:Arabic geomantic signs, wheel of life and death, the zodiac Wellcome V0025818ER.jpg
entries.summary: A European engraving depicting Arabic geomantic signs alongside a wheel of life and death and zodiac symbols, from the Wellcome Collection's iconographic collections. The engraving places the 16 geomantic figures in tabular form alongside circular diagrams — a zodiac wheel and a life/death wheel — demonstrating how Islamic geomancy was understood and represented in European occult literature. By the 17th–18th century, raml had entered European geomancy texts (including those by Robert Fludd and Christopher Cattan) as 'geomantia', where the Arabic figures were transliterated with Latin names (Albus, Puer, Cauda Draconis, etc.). This image documents the transmission of Islamic divinatory science into European esoteric tradition.

entries.title: Arabic Diagram of Geomantic Figures Classification (15th c., from Madagascar)
entries.place: Madagascar (Arabic geomantic tradition in the Indian Ocean world)
entries.rights: Public domain. Sourced from OpenEdition Journals (L'Homme).
entries.summary: A 15th-century Arabic diagram from Madagascar showing a classification of the geomantic figures (al-ashkal), demonstrating the remarkable geographical reach of Islamic raml. Geomancy arrived in Madagascar with Arab and Swahili traders and became the sikidy, a local divination system that adapted the 16 Islamic geomantic figures to a bamboo-stalk binary reading system. This diagram shows the figures in their classification scheme — probably grouped by element (fire, air, water, earth) and associated characteristics (entering/exiting, fortunate/unfortunate). The document evidences the transmission of Islamic occult science across the Indian Ocean trade networks, where it merged with indigenous divination traditions throughout coastal East Africa and the islands.
